```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  # move2utils is a suggested package, available from GitHub
  eval = requireNamespace("move2utils", quietly = TRUE)
)
```

[`move2utils`](https://move2universe.github.io/move2utils/) (Kranstauber,
Safi & Scharf) is a package of utility functions for `move2` objects, with
methods for outlier detection, thinning, corridor detection and Brownian
bridge utilisation distributions. As `tidytracks` is also built on `move2`,
it can use these methods directly. `tidytracks` provides wrappers that follow
its own conventions: functions starting with `event_` return one value per
event, `tt_` functions return the modified tibble of tracks, `track_`
functions return one value per track, and `hr_tt_` functions estimate home
ranges. Physical quantities are given as `units` objects, and events without
a location are handled as in the rest of `tidytracks`.

| `tidytracks` | `move2utils` |
|---|---|
| `max_speed_allometric()` | `v_phys_estimate()` |
| `track_suggest_max_speed()` | `mt_suggest_speed_cap()` |
| `event_flag_outliers()`, `tt_clean_outliers()` | `mt_clean_track()`, `mt_flag_speed_cap()`, `mt_flag_outliers_detour()`, `mt_flag_outliers_bridge()`, `mt_flag_outliers()` |
| `event_flag_thin_time()`, `tt_thin_time()` | `mt_thin_time()` |
| `event_flag_thin_distance()`, `tt_thin_distance()` | `mt_thin_distance()` |
| `event_flag_corridor()` | `mt_corridor()` |
| `hr_tt_dbbmm()`, `hr_tt_dbgb()` | `mt_dbbmm_ud()`, `mt_dbgb_ud()` |
| `event_ud_level()` | `ud_outer_probability()` |
| `hr_tt_ud_overlap(method = "earth_mover_sinkhorn")` | `emd()` |

`move2utils` is not on CRAN; install it from GitHub with:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("move2universe/move2utils")
```

## The data

We use the Antarctic shag tracks from the main `tidytracks` vignette
(`vignette("tidytracks")`). Remember that these data were modified to show
the functionality of `tidytracks`, and should not be used for analyses of shag
movement.

```{r read_data, message = FALSE}
library(tidytracks)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)

shags_tt <- tt_read_data(
  events = system.file("extdata", "shags_example.csv", package = "tidytracks"),
  col_track_id = "bird_id",
  col_coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  col_date_time = "date_time",
  time_zone = "UTC",
  crs = 4326
)
```

Most `move2utils` methods work on the steps between consecutive events, so the
wrappers require the events to be ordered by time within each track. If they
are not, they give an error suggesting `tt_order_time()`:

```{r order}
shags_tt <- shags_tt %>% tt_order_time()
```

We will also need a metric projection for some of the analyses:

```{r projection}
shags_crs <- paste0(
  "+proj=aeqd +lon_0=-68 +lat_0=-67 ",
  "+units=m +datum=WGS84 +no_defs"
)
```

## Choosing a maximum speed

Speed filters such as `tt_clean_mcconnell()` need a maximum speed. When no
published value is available for a species, `max_speed_allometric()` predicts
the maximum speed of an animal from its body mass and mode of locomotion
(Hirt et al. 2017). For a flying bird of about 2.5 kg:

```{r allometric}
max_speed_allometric(as_units(2.5, "kg"), mode = "flying") %>%
  set_units("km/h")
```

This is a ceiling on what an animal of that mass can physically do, and here
it is about twice the 58 km/h observed for shags: a published, species-specific
value (as used in the main vignette) should be preferred when available.

Alternatively, `track_suggest_max_speed()` looks, in each track, for a break in
the distribution of speeds between plausible steps and outliers:

```{r suggest_speed}
track_suggest_max_speed(shags_tt, units = as_units("km/h"))
```

No break was found for most tracks (`NA`), and the suggestions for the others
vary widely: for `kb_38`, which hardly moved, the break is more likely to
separate resting from moving than plausible steps from outliers. Data-driven
suggestions must always be checked against the biology of the species.

## Detecting outliers

`event_flag_outliers()` detects outliers with one of the methods of
`move2utils`, returning `TRUE` for valid events (as `event_flag_mcconnell()`
does). Further arguments are passed to the `move2utils` function, with `units`
objects converted to the units it expects. Let us compare McConnell's filter
with three of these methods: a hard speed cap at the same maximum speed, the
detour ratio (which flags out-and-back spikes, here ignoring legs shorter than
100 m to avoid flagging GPS jitter while resting), and `mt_clean_track()`, the
default, which combines several methods and chooses its thresholds from the
data:

```{r outliers}
shags_flags <- shags_tt %>%
  mutate(
    mcconnell = event_flag_mcconnell(., max_speed = as_units(60, "km/h")),
    speed_cap = event_flag_outliers(
      .,
      method = "speed_cap",
      v_max = as_units(60, "km/h"),
      threshold_type = "hard"
    ),
    detour = event_flag_outliers(
      .,
      method = "detour",
      min_leg = as_units(100, "m")
    ),
    clean_track = event_flag_outliers(.)
  )

shags_flags %>%
  as.data.frame(drop_geometry = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(across(c(mcconnell, speed_cap, detour, clean_track), ~ sum(!.x)))
```

The methods flag different numbers of events. Let us look at where they are,
for three of the birds:

```{r plot_outliers, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 8}
shags_flags_long <- shags_flags %>%
  filter(bird_id %in% c("kb_19", "kb_27", "kb_42")) %>%
  st_transform(shags_crs) %>%
  mutate(
    x = st_coordinates(.)[, 1],
    y = st_coordinates(.)[, 2]
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame(drop_geometry = TRUE) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    c(mcconnell, speed_cap, detour, clean_track),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "valid"
  )

ggplot(shags_flags_long, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(
    data = filter(shags_flags_long, !valid),
    colour = "red",
    size = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_grid(method ~ bird_id, scales = "free") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())
```

All methods detect the isolated locations far from the rest of the track. The
speed cap flags the events on both sides of every step faster than 60 km/h,
whilst McConnell's filter keeps steps that are only just too fast. With its
default settings, however, `mt_clean_track()` also flags whole stretches of
slow, dense movement of these frequently sampled birds (e.g. `kb_19` and
`kb_42`). Whatever the method, it is important to look at the flagged events
before removing them. To inspect the diagnostics of a `move2utils` method, call
it directly on the tibble of tracks, e.g.
`move2utils::mt_clean_track(shags_tt, remove = FALSE)`.

`tt_clean_outliers()` acts on the outliers in the same ways as
`tt_clean_mcconnell()`, e.g. replacing their location by interpolation:

```{r clean_outliers}
shags_interpolated <- shags_tt %>%
  tt_clean_outliers(
    method = "speed_cap",
    v_max = as_units(60, "km/h"),
    threshold_type = "hard",
    flag_action = "interpolate"
  )
nrow(shags_interpolated) == nrow(shags_tt)
```

For the rest of this article, we use McConnell's filter, as in the main
vignette:

```{r mcconnell}
shags_clean <- shags_tt %>%
  tt_clean_mcconnell(max_speed = as_units(60, "km/h"))
```

## Thinning tracks

`tt_regular_time()` resamples tracks to a regular interval by interpolating new
locations. To keep the original locations instead, `tt_thin_time()` keeps the
largest subset of events whose intervals are within a tolerance of the target
interval (by default, a tenth of it):

```{r thin_time}
shags_10min <- shags_clean %>%
  tt_thin_time(interval = as_units(10, "min"))
nrow(shags_clean)
nrow(shags_10min)
summary(event_interval(shags_10min, units = as_units("min")))
```

The longer intervals are gaps in the data, which thinning never bridges.

`tt_thin_distance()` thins tracks by the distance travelled along them; by
default, it keeps an event every time the bird has travelled at least the
given distance since the last kept event:

```{r thin_distance}
shags_500m <- shags_clean %>%
  tt_thin_distance(distance = as_units(500, "m"))
nrow(shags_500m)
```

The corresponding `event_flag_thin_time()` and `event_flag_thin_distance()`
flag the events to keep, without removing the others.

## Movement corridors

`event_flag_corridor()` flags the steps that are part of corridors: steps that
are fast, and surrounded by other fast steps running in a similar direction
(in either direction along the corridor). The thresholds are estimated from the
data if not given, but explicit values make results comparable among datasets:

```{r corridor, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
shags_corridor <- shags_clean %>%
  st_transform(shags_crs) %>%
  mutate(
    corridor = event_flag_corridor(
      .,
      speed_threshold = as_units(30, "km/h"),
      circvar_threshold = 0.2
    )
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_event_path(data = shags_corridor, aes(colour = corridor)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey60", `TRUE` = "red"))
```

## Home ranges with Brownian bridges

Unlike kernel density estimation (`hr_tt_kde()`), which treats locations as
independent, dynamic Brownian bridge movement models (dBBMM) model the
movement between consecutive locations, weighting the utilisation distribution
(UD) by time. `hr_tt_dbbmm()` estimates the UD of each track (`hr_tt_dbgb()`
does the same with dynamic bivariate Gaussian bridges). As bridges link
consecutive events of a track, the data must be ungrouped, or grouped by
track.

Following the main vignette, we split the tracks into foraging trips (so that
bridges do not span the long periods spent at the colony), keep the females,
and project the data:

```{r trips}
show_meta(shags_clean) <- show_meta(shags_clean) %>%
  mutate(colony_coord = sf_point_col(colony_lon, colony_lat, crs = 4326))

shags_females <- shags_clean %>%
  tt_split_trips(
    centre_col = "colony_coord",
    buffer_outbound = as_units(3, "km"),
    buffer_inbound = as_units(3, "km"),
    complete = TRUE
  ) %>%
  filter_by_meta(sex == "female") %>%
  st_transform(shags_crs)
```

We now estimate a UD for each trip. The location error of the GPS fixes is set
to 20 m and, with a location every 2 minutes, we use a sliding window of 15
locations (30 minutes) to estimate the motion variance. The grid must be large
enough to contain the bridges, and fine enough relative to their width (the
densities are evaluated at the centres of the cells); we give a grid with a
margin of about 5 km around the locations and a resolution of 50 m:

```{r dbbmm}
shags_grid <- c(xmin = -15000, ymin = -68000, xmax = 18000, ymax = -31000)

trips_dbbmm <- shags_females %>%
  hr_tt_dbbmm(
    location_error = as_units(20, "m"),
    window_size = 15,
    margin = 5,
    bbox = shags_grid,
    res = 50
  )
trips_dbbmm
```

The result is an `hr_tt_ud_tbl`, as returned by `hr_tt_kde()`, so it can be
used with the other `hr_tt_ud_*()` functions. For example, we can combine the
trips of each bird with `hr_tt_ud_sum()`:

```{r dbbmm_birds}
birds_dbbmm <- trips_dbbmm %>%
  left_join(
    show_meta(shags_females) %>% select(trip_id, bird_id),
    by = "trip_id"
  ) %>%
  mutate(bird_id = as.character(bird_id)) %>%
  group_by(bird_id) %>%
  hr_tt_ud_sum()
birds_dbbmm
```

Let us compare these UDs with kernel UDs estimated on the same grid:

```{r kde}
birds_kde <- shags_females %>%
  group_by(bird_id) %>%
  hr_tt_kde(bbox = shags_grid, res = 50)
```

As both are on the same grid, we can compute their overlap for each bird
(here with Bhattacharyya's affinity):

```{r overlap}
tibble(
  bird_id = birds_dbbmm$bird_id,
  overlap = purrr::map2_dbl(
    birds_dbbmm$ud,
    birds_kde$ud,
    hr_tt_ud_overlap
  )
)
```

The overlap is low: with accurate, frequent locations, the bridges are narrow,
and the dBBMM UDs are concentrated along the paths and where the birds spent
most time, whilst the kernel UDs spread around every location. Plotting the
50% and 95% isopleths of one bird:

```{r plot_isopleths, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
kb_42_iso <- bind_rows(
  hr_tt_ud_iso(birds_dbbmm, levels = c(0.5, 0.95)),
  hr_tt_ud_iso(birds_kde, levels = c(0.5, 0.95))
) %>%
  filter(bird_id == "kb_42") %>%
  mutate(level = factor(level))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = kb_42_iso,
    aes(colour = method, linetype = level),
    fill = NA
  ) +
  geom_event_point(
    data = filter(shags_females, bird_id == "kb_42"),
    size = 0.5
  )
```

`event_ud_level()` gives, for each event, the level of the smallest isopleth of
a UD that contains it (from 0 in the core to 1 at the edge). With a table of
UDs, each event is matched to the UD of its own row, here its bird:

```{r ud_level}
shags_females %>%
  mutate(ud_level = event_ud_level(., birds_dbbmm)) %>%
  as.data.frame(drop_geometry = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(bird_id) %>%
  summarise(in_core = mean(ud_level <= 0.5))
```

Finally, the Earth Mover's Distance measures how far apart two UDs are (in the
units of the projection, here metres). `method = "earth_mover_sinkhorn"`
computes a fast approximation, which scales to large grids:

```{r emd}
hr_tt_ud_overlap(birds_dbbmm, method = "earth_mover_sinkhorn")
```

## References

Hirt, M. R., Jetz, W., Rall, B. C. & Brose, U. (2017). A general scaling law
reveals why the largest animals are not the fastest. *Nature Ecology &
Evolution*, 1, 1116-1122.

Kranstauber, B., Kays, R., LaPoint, S. D., Wikelski, M. & Safi, K. (2012). A
dynamic Brownian bridge movement model to estimate utilization distributions
for heterogeneous animal movement. *Journal of Animal Ecology*, 81, 738-746.

Kranstauber, B., Safi, K. & Scharf, A. K. (2026). move2utils: a utility
toolkit for the move2 ecosystem. *bioRxiv*.
<https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.07.736908>
